title: Introduction to Azure Key Vault
description: Understand why secrets should not live in code and how Key Vault secures them.

data.text: Hardcoded connection strings, API keys, and certificates are one of the most common security vulnerabilities in .NET applications. Azure Key Vault stores these secrets in a managed, encrypted service.

items: **Secrets** — strings such as database connection strings and API keys
**Keys** — cryptographic keys for encryption and signing
**Certificates** — TLS certificates imported from CA providers or self-signed

rows: One vault per environment with RBAC
Manual secret updates in every app

data.title: Never commit secrets
data.text: Even in private repos, secrets should not be committed. Use Key Vault, environment variables, or Azure App Configuration with managed identity.

data.title: Create a Key Vault with Azure CLI
data.content: Create a Key Vault in the same region as your App Service.
data.code:
az keyvault create \
  --name aspnet-azure-kv \
  --resource-group azure-for-aspnet-rg \
  --location eastus \
  --enable-rbac-authorization true

az keyvault secret set --vault-name aspnet-azure-kv --name "ConnectionStrings--Default" --value "Server=tcp:..."

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Key Vault replaces hardcoded secrets with centrally managed values
Access is controlled by Azure RBAC and policies
Secrets can be referenced by Azure App Service and ASP.NET Core configuration
Key Vault supports auditing, rotation, and geo-replication
data.takeaway: Key Vault is the first step in moving secrets out of your code and into a purpose-built Azure service.
